clips.text_zh: 又睇到呢張圖。$1,000 放15年 BTC 變 $8.97M、NVDA $735K、TSLA $231K、AAPL $29K、SPX $8.4K、金 $2.15K。問自己 2026 應該瞓邊隻。🙏
clips.text_en_b1: Here is a return chart from a /biz/ thread. One thousand dollars invested 15 years ago today would be worth: Bitcoin $8,970,000, Nvidia $735,000, Tesla $231,000, Apple $29,000, the S&P $8,400, and Gold $2,150. The post asks which asset you would have picked.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ compares BTC vs NVDA vs TSLA vs gold over 15 years

signal.rationale: Retro performance chart, not a forward trade

clips.text_en_b2: A /biz/ chart illustrates the absurd scale of long-term returns. A thousand dollars invested fifteen years back would now be worth around 8.97 million in Bitcoin, 735K in Nvidia, 231K in Tesla, 29K in Apple, 8.4K in the S&P, and a mere 2,150 in gold. While hindsight is twenty-twenty, the poster poses the inevitable question: which of these assets should one be holding into 2026, given such staggering historical performance?
clips.text_en_c1: A circulating infographic from a /biz/ thread illustrates the hypothetical fifteen-year appreciation of a thousand-dollar position across several asset classes. Bitcoin would have compounded to roughly 8.97 million dollars, whereas Nvidia, Tesla, Apple, the S&P 500, and gold would have yielded approximately 735,000, 231,000, 29,000, 8,400, and 2,150 dollars respectively. The original poster, evidently in a reflective mood, poses a pointed rhetorical question: which of these instruments ought one to have held through to the present? The thread invites readers to interrogate their own conviction, risk appetite, and capacity to endure volatility over the long horizon.
clips.text_en_c2: A return-comparison graphic circulating on the /biz/ subforum lays bare the extraordinary divergence in fifteen-year asset performance: a single thousand dollars deployed in 2010 would, by present reckoning, have compounded into roughly 8.97 million in Bitcoin, 735,000 in Nvidia, 231,000 in Tesla, a comparatively modest 29,000 in Apple, 8,400 in the S&P 500 index, and a barely-inflation-matching 2,150 in physical gold. The closing provocation—essentially a prompt to speculate ex post facto on which vehicle one ought to have slept through the volatility holding—is, of course, classic hindsight theatre. Yet the underlying arithmetic is bracing: a diversified equity-and-bullion portfolio would have underperformed a single volatile cryptocurrency by nearly four orders of magnitude, a fact that quietly indicts conventional portfolio construction while flattering the chancer's intuition.

clips.text_zh: Cybercab 迷思帖。買一架放入 Tesla Robotaxi 網路等收 passive income。又係 Elon 嘅嘢，識條鐵咩。🧐 講就易，做就...
clips.text_en_b1: A bizzer wants to be redpilled on buying Tesla Cybercabs and putting them to work on the Tesla Robotaxi network for passive income. The thread asks /biz/ whether this is actually a real side hustle or pure hopium. Many replies say no normal person can buy them yet.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ anon asks about Tesla Cybercab passive income

signal.rationale: Robotaxi network uptake is a long-dated TSLA bull case but no clear entry trigger

clips.text_en_b2: A bizzer is seeking honest takes on whether buying a Tesla Cybercab and plugging it into the Robotaxi network constitutes a genuine passive-income side hustle, or whether it amounts to little more than hopium and vapour. The consensus forming in the thread is fairly blunt: ordinary retail buyers cannot yet get their hands on the units, so any returns remain purely hypothetical for the foreseeable future.
clips.text_en_c1: A thread on /biz/ invites respondents to demystify the prospective Tesla Cybercab scheme, whereby an ordinary retail buyer would acquire one or more units and deploy them within the forthcoming Tesla Robotaxi network in pursuit of largely passive returns. Scepticism abounds, as several anons contend that retail access remains, for the time being, a pipedream, and that the entire proposition smacks of hopium rather than grounded enterprise. Others concede that, should Elon Musk's broader autonomy roadmap materialise, the model could in principle yield meaningful residual income, though the practical barriers to entry render such speculation, for most, premature.
clips.text_en_c2: A /biz/ interlocutor, evidently still awaiting edification, is requesting red-pilling on the proposition that one might acquire Tesla Cybercab units and consign them to the forthcoming Robotaxi network in hopes of accruing passive income. The thread's prevailing scepticism is grounded in mundane operational reality: the vehicles are not yet purchasable by ordinary retail participants, deployment timelines remain deliberately vague, and any yield projection rests on assumptions that Musk-adjacent marketing has been characteristically reluctant to substantiate. Replies skew derisive, dismissing the entire proposition as hopium—an elegant bit of /biz/ patois denoting fantasies that feel like investment theses. Several anons point out that fleet economics, insurance liability, regulatory clearance, and utilisation rates constitute unresolved questions that glossy keynote imagery does not answer.

clips.text_en_b2: OpenAI has officially rolled out GPT-6 Astra, framing it as the most capable and aligned model yet and formally ushering in what they call the AGI era. Benchmark results show the system nearly saturating ARC-AGI 3, while the wider /g/ thread treats the launch as a genuinely seismic moment for the industry, one that renders a growing chunk of white-collar studying arguably obsolete.
clips.text_en_c1: OpenAI has formally unveiled GPT-6 Astra, billing it as the most capable and best-aligned system the organisation has yet produced, and effectively heralding what its marketing apparatus describes as the dawn of the AGI era. Internal benchmarks suggest the model comes perilously close to saturating ARC-AGI 3, a result that several /g/ commentators interpret as a watershed moment for the industry. One anonymous poster, evidently in the throes of licensing-exam preparation, laments that any competitive edge afforded by rote study may soon be rendered obsolete, and asks, half-seriously, whether AI itself might constitute the only viable liferaft.
clips.text_en_c2: OpenAI has formally unveiled GPT-6 Astra, marketing the system as its most capable and aligned model to date and, with characteristic restraint, heralding the advent of the AGI era. Internal benchmarks purport to show the model approaching saturation on ARC-AGI 3, a metric once considered a credible yardstick for general reasoning. Across parallel /g/ threads, the release is being treated less as an incremental improvement than as an industry-shattering inflection point—a nuclear moment, as several posters have phrased it, for both commercial competitors and white-collar labour markets writ large. The prevailing anxiety, articulated with typical /g/ fatalism, concerns the diminishing viability of credentialed human expertise: if reasoning benchmarks plateau, what remains that a sufficiently motivated model cannot eventually subsume?

clips.text_en_b1: A /pol/ thread says that once China rules New Zealand, they should ban the haka, calling it the cringiest thing from that part of the world. The poster wonders how any white man from NZ could think the haka is cool or join in, and questions why the British did not just shoot all of those savages.
clips.source_hint: /pol/ rant trashing the haka and NZ

signal.rationale: Culture war post, no market angle

clips.text_en_b2: A /pol/ poster claims that once China gains political control of New Zealand, the haka should be banned outright, branding it the cringiest cultural export from that region. They further wonder how any white New Zealander could genuinely find the ritual cool enough to participate in, and question why British colonisers failed to simply eliminate the people behind such an absurd performance. The whole thread reads like a parody.
clips.text_en_c1: A particularly inflammatory /pol/ thread posits that, were New Zealand ever to fall under Chinese administration, the haka should be prohibited outright, with the poster dismissing the ceremonial performance as the most cringeworthy cultural export from that region. The same contributor professes bafflement at any white New Zealander who might find the ritual compelling, let alone elect to participate, and further muses that the British ought, in hindsight, to have simply liquidated the indigenous population during the colonial era. The remarks, predictably, draw condemnation from those familiar with the tradition's martial and ceremonial gravity.
clips.text_en_c2: A /pol/ thread, having apparently exhausted its reserves of sober analysis, has alighted upon the proposition that once Chinese dominion descends upon New Zealand, the indigenous Māori haka ought to be proscribed. The poster, displaying the customary detachment for which that board is renowned, additionally muses on how any self-respecting Pākehā could find the ceremonial dance aesthetically tolerable, let alone elect to perform it, before ruminating on whether the British ought not to have resorted to more terminal colonial solutions. The contribution is, predictably, less interested in ethnographic nuance than in provocation for its own sake. For anyone raised within a British colonial milieu—and the present observer qualifies—this particular brand of historical humour curdles rather quickly, trading in cruelty for the sake of transgressive amusement.

clips.text_zh: /v/ 講有隻 eroge 喺 Steam Japan 排第一，勁過晒啲 AAA PC game。LOL 都係日本 trend 食緊 — S15 都唔知觀唔觀眾有冇被搶走。🧐
clips.text_en_b1: A /v/ poster points out that an eroge is currently ranked number one on Steam in Japan. They ask how an eroge sold more than any AAA game on PC in Japan. Replies point to the smaller market size and the niche release style of Japanese PC eroge titles lately.
clips.source_hint: /v/ shocked that an eroge tops the Japan Steam chart
clips.text_en_b2: A /v/ poster flags a genuinely surprising development on the Japanese Steam charts: an eroge has knocked every major AAA PC release off the top spot in the region. Repliers point to the comparatively small size of the Japanese PC market and the niche, staggered release windows of domestic eroge titles, arguing that scaling context rather than raw popularity explains the headline. Still, League of Legends viewership keeps declining.
clips.text_en_c1: A /v/ observer notes, with no small measure of incredulity, that an adult visual novel currently occupies the number-one position on Steam's Japanese regional charts, eclipsing every major AAA PC release of the season. The original poster queries how such a niche title could conceivably outperform productions backed by substantially larger marketing budgets. Responding anons attribute the anomaly to the comparatively modest scale of the Japanese PC market, alongside the increasingly curated, almost boutique-style release cadence that has come to characterise domestic eroge publishing in recent quarters.
clips.text_en_c2: A /v/ correspondent has observed what appears to be a genuine market anomaly: an eroge currently occupies the top slot on Steam's Japanese charts, eclipsing every AAA PC release in the domestic market. The rhetorical question—how a title from a comparatively marginal genre can outsell productions budgeted at orders of magnitude greater—is less naïve than it first appears, since the answer lies partly in the structural peculiarities of Japanese PC distribution. Niche eroge publishers exploit tight release windows, aggressive bundling, and a devout enthusiast base that conventional Western-style blockbuster marketing cannot replicate. The discussion has, predictably, wandered into adjacent anxieties: whether League of Legends viewership, itself buoyed by the S15 cycle, is itself cannibalising mainstream engagement.

clips.text_en_b2: A /fit/ regular wants to overhaul their training setup and is asking the board for help putting together a fresh five-or-six-day plan. clips.text_en_c1: A /fit/ regular solicits guidance on restructuring their regimen into a five- or six-day programme, having grown weary of the Jeff Nippard Powerbuilding template they have been following for some months. Particular fatigue is directed at deadlifts and hip thrusts, while an underutilised heavy bag at their facility has prompted interest in a hybrid protocol that interleaves resistance work with striking sessions and dedicated cardio blocks. Currently in a cutting phase, they concede that their overhead press has yet to clear a single plate, a detail many respondents seize upon as they recalibrate the suggested programme.
clips.text_en_c2: A /fit/ participant, evidently wearied of Jeff Nippard's Powerbuilding programme after extended adherence, has solicited guidance on constructing a five-to-six-day hybrid regimen that integrates conventional resistance work with heavy-bag training and cardiovascular conditioning. Their gym's heavy bag languishes untouched, presenting an opportunity they intend to exploit, while their current pressing numbers—a one-plate overhead press that remains aspirational—suggest they are mid-cut and unwilling to sacrifice muscle for the sake of leaning out prematurely. Deadlifts and hip thrusts, predictably, have lost their charm. The underlying impulse is one familiar to seasoned lifters: periodisation fatigue, the creeping suspicion that marginal returns have flattened, and a yearning for the metabolic brutality that only striking work reliably delivers when the barbell has begun to feel like a chore.

clips.text_en_b1: A first-time watcher of Demon Slayer is on season 2 and asks why so many people online hate on it. They say the criticism also applies to other beloved anime, so it might just be backlash because KnY made billions. The thread is half-defending, half-dunking the show.

clips.text_en_b2: A first-time Demon Slayer viewer, now deep into season two, is pushing back against the relentless online criticism the show attracts. They argue that similar complaints get levelled at plenty of other beloved anime, suggesting the hate stems largely from backlash against KnY's enormous commercial success rather than any genuine flaw. clips.text_en_c1: A first-time viewer of Demon Slayer, presently midway through the second season, turns to /a/ seeking an explanation for the disproportionate vitriol the series attracts online. They observe, not unreasonably, that comparable criticisms could be levelled at numerous acclaimed titles whose merits remain largely uncontested, and speculate that the hostility may stem less from any genuine aesthetic deficiency than from the sheer commercial ubiquity of a franchise that has generated billions in revenue. The thread consequently fractures between respondents mounting earnest defences of the adaptation and others content merely to dunk upon it.
clips.text_en_c2: A first-time viewer of Demon Slayer, having progressed into the second season, has ventured onto /a/ to inquire why the franchise attracts such disproportionate online contempt. Their defence is elegantly reductive: the same criticisms levelled at KnY—derivative plotting, archetypal protagonists, structurally conventional arcs—apply with equal force to beloved fixtures of the medium, suggesting that the hostility is less aesthetic than sociological. A series that grosses billions invites a backlash commensurate with its success, regardless of intrinsic merit. The thread's contributors split accordingly, half offering qualified defences, half piling on with reflexive contrarianism. One poster, self-identifying as a Gundam 00 alumnus who favours engineering-inflected narratives, confesses to consuming KnY purely as a visual experience—an honourable compromise, if not an outright endorsement.
